# Incident Report — Malware Infection, Host 10.1.21.58 (DESKTOP-ES9F3ML)

**Evidence reviewed:** `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 frames, 26.4 MB). No IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence directory — only the pcap.

## 1. Victim host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.1.21.58** |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** (Intel NIC) |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** (NetBIOS domain/workgroup name: WIN11OFFICE, AD domain win11office.com) |
| Logged-in Windows user | **gwyatt** (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ CNameString exchanges with the domain controller at 10.1.21.2) |

Identified via DHCP Option 12 hostname (`DESKTOP-ES9F3ML`), NBNS name registrations, and Kerberos traffic pairing the host IP with the `gwyatt` principal against realm `WIN11OFFICE.COM`.

## 2. Malware family

**Behavioral attribution only — not signature-confirmed.** No IDS/AV alerts were provided with this evidence, and the actual payload/stealer binary was never observed in cleartext (final delivery occurred over TLS, which cannot be decrypted without a keylog). Based on traffic behavior, this matches a **commodity loader/infostealer delivered via a fake-download-site + TDS fingerprinting gate chain** (the pattern commonly associated with SEO-poisoning-driven stealer campaigns, e.g. Lumma/Vidar-class loaders using a browser-fingerprinting gate before final payload/exfil). I cannot name a specific family with certainty from network evidence alone — this should be confirmed with an EDR/AV scan or memory forensics on the host.

## 3. Timeline of the infection chain (all times as captured, +0400)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 03:04:49.017 | `www.google.com` query from victim (search) |
| 03:04:49.225 | DNS: **hiyter.com** → 104.21.22.231 / 172.67.207.145 (Cloudflare-fronted) |
| 03:04:49.756 | DNS: **media.megafilehub4.lat** → 104.21.48.156 / 172.67.154.67 |
| 03:04:52.194 | DNS: **arch.filemegahab4.sbs** → 104.21.46.67 / 172.67.136.13 |
| 03:04:49.86–50.7+ | TLS session to 104.21.48.156:443 (SNI `media.megafilehub4.lat`), **~50 KB up / ~166 KB down** — consistent with stager/payload retrieval from the fake file-hosting page |
| 03:05:34.196 | DNS: **whooptm.cyou** → 62.72.32.156 |
| 03:05:36.219 | DNS: **whitepepper.su** → 153.92.1.49 |
| 03:05:38.518–03:05:47.7 | HTTP GET/POST cycle to `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49:80) — browser-fingerprinting/bot-check gate (see §4) |
| 03:06:06.713 | DNS: **holiday-forever.cc** → 80.97.160.24 |
| 03:06:10.453 | DNS: **communicationfirewall-security.cc** → 104.21.9.36 / 172.67.141.109 |
| ~03:05:34–03:06:15 | Multiple upload-heavy TLS sessions to 80.97.160.24:443 (**119 KB up / 5.5 KB down**) and 104.21.9.36:443 (**102 KB up / 5 KB down**, second stream 34 KB up / 12 KB down) — the outbound-heavy byte ratio is consistent with data being exfiltrated *to* these hosts rather than content being downloaded |

## 4. C2/gate behavior confirmed in cleartext

`whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49) served plaintext HTTP on port 80 and is the clearest grounded artifact in this capture:

- **GET** `/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome` (repeated again with `agent=Edge`)
- Server returned an HTML page containing JavaScript that fingerprints the browser: `navigator` properties, WebGL vendor/renderer, canvas fingerprint hash, screen metrics, connection info, timezone.
- **POST** `.../set_agent?...&act=log` — the client uploaded the full fingerprint JSON (~8 KB) back to the server.
- Server response to the log POST: literal text **`cant open archive 172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1.zip`** — indicating the gate maintains a per-victim archive keyed by public IP + a hash/token, and failed to hand it off in this session (public/WAN IP 172.56.88.98 does not match the LAN capture, confirming NAT egress).
- This exact request/response pattern (id/token/agent fingerprint → act=log → per-IP zip archive lookup) is a **traffic-distribution-system (TDS) fingerprint gate**, typically used to vet real human/Windows browsers before releasing a payload archive — a known pattern in malvertising/SEO-poisoning stealer campaigns.
- The host also repeatedly re-established short TLS sessions (443) to 153.92.1.49 roughly once per second across the same window — consistent with beacon/poll behavior from the gate page while waiting on the server-side decision.

## 5. Indicators of Compromise

**Domains (all resolved by the victim during the infection window):**
- `hiyter.com`
- `media.megafilehub4.lat`
- `arch.filemegahab4.sbs`
- `whooptm.cyou`
- `whitepepper.su`
- `holiday-forever.cc`
- `communicationfirewall-security.cc`

**C2 / malicious endpoints (IP:port):**
- `153.92.1.49:80` and `153.92.1.49:443` — whitepepper.su (fingerprinting gate, confirmed cleartext C2 traffic)
- `104.21.48.156:443` — media.megafilehub4.lat (Cloudflare-fronted, download-heavy — likely stager/payload delivery)
- `104.21.46.67:443` — arch.filemegahab4.sbs (Cloudflare-fronted)
- `62.72.32.156:443` — whooptm.cyou
- `80.97.160.24:443` — holiday-forever.cc (upload-heavy — likely exfil)
- `104.21.9.36:443` — communicationfirewall-security.cc (upload-heavy — likely exfil)
- `104.21.22.231:443` — hiyter.com

**Malicious URLs (confirmed cleartext HTTP):**
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log`
- `http://whitepepper.su/favicon.ico`

**Bot/victim identifiers issued by the gate:**
- id: `3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C`
- token: `842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b`
- referenced archive name: `172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1.zip` (172.56.88.98 = victim's public/WAN egress IP, not a C2 IP itself)

**Transferred files / hashes:** None could be extracted. No PE, script, or archive was ever seen in cleartext HTTP in this capture — every candidate payload transfer (media.megafilehub4.lat, whooptm.cyou, holiday-forever.cc, communicationfirewall-security.cc) occurred over TLS 1.2/1.3 with no keylog available, so file names and SHA256 hashes cannot be derived from this pcap alone. Full packet capture with `SSLKEYLOGFILE` or an endpoint/EDR triage of DESKTOP-ES9F3ML is required to recover the actual binary and compute a hash.

## 6. Assessment

Host **10.1.21.58 / DESKTOP-ES9F3ML**, logged in as **gwyatt**, followed a Google search result to `hiyter.com`, pivoted through a fake file-hosting domain pair (`media.megafilehub4.lat`, `arch.filemegahab4.sbs`) that served a stager/downloader over TLS, then was routed through a TDS/fingerprinting gate at `whitepepper.su` that fingerprinted the browser and logged the result, and finally exhibited upload-heavy TLS sessions to `holiday-forever.cc` and `communicationfirewall-security.cc` consistent with data exfiltration. This is the network signature of a commodity stealer/loader delivered via SEO-poisoning malvertising; specific family attribution requires host-side (EDR/AV/memory) analysis since no payload hash was recoverable from network traffic alone.

**Recommended next steps:** isolate 10.1.21.58, block the domains/IPs above at the perimeter, run an offline AV/EDR scan and memory capture on the host to recover and hash the actual binary, and force credential resets for the `gwyatt` account given the apparent exfil activity.
